domains.name: AI Insurance
domains.blurb:
Insurance is where AI risk stops being a principle and acquires a price. An underwriter has to decide what a model failure costs, whether a coolant leak in a liquid-cooled rack is a property claim or an equipment breakdown, and whether a policy written before generative AI existed still covers what the insured is now doing with it. Those decisions are being made now, mostly quietly, and they will shape deployment more directly than most published guidance.

This hub tracks both directions. How insurers use AI in underwriting and claims, and, more consequentially for the industry, how the insurance market prices the AI and data centre buildout: property and business interruption on facilities, errors and omissions on model outputs, cyber cover for prompt injection and model extraction, intellectual property defence for training data, supply chain cover on chips and transformers, and the actuarial problem of pricing a risk with no claims history.

Ten sections, each tracking a distinct part of the value chain.

sections.name: Physical Infrastructure and Property
sections.blurb: Property cover on the buildings themselves. Liquid cooling leaks, transformer and substation failures under sudden AI load, battery storage fire risk, structural floor loading on racks above 100 kW, water use and environmental impairment, small modular reactor co-location, physical sabotage, and how reinsurers price site selection.

sections.name: Business Interruption and Power Grid
sections.blurb: What a stoppage costs and who pays. Utility load shedding and throttling, contingent business interruption when a hyperscaler outage freezes downstream applications, subsea cable cuts, GPU provider service level breaches, power purchase agreement failures, foundational API outages, drought-driven water shutoffs, and interconnection queue delay.

sections.name: Model Liability and Errors and Omissions
sections.blurb: Cover for what a model does. Algorithmic bias class actions in hiring, lending and tenant screening, autonomous agents executing bad transactions, diagnostic AI malpractice, hallucinated professional advice, autonomous vehicle product liability, trading bot losses, industrial control misconfiguration, chatbot defamation and unauthorised commitments, coding assistant vulnerabilities, and deepfake wire fraud.

sections.name: Intellectual Property and Copyright
sections.blurb: The training data question, priced. Copyright infringement defence for developers facing class actions, output ownership and patent invalidity, scraping under GDPR and CCPA, trade secret contamination from code entering public training sets, how hyperscaler IP indemnities hold up against actual policy conditions, provenance failures, open weight licence non-compliance, right of publicity, and cross-border scraping jurisdiction.

sections.name: Cyber, Data Breach and Prompt Injection
sections.blurb: Where cyber policy language meets attacks that did not exist when it was written. Indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration, model inversion and training data extraction, operational technology ransomware on building controls, supply chain malware in public model hubs, model poisoning, shadow AI exfiltration, biometric spoofing, API key theft and compute hijacking, zero days in open source stacks, and how act of war exclusions apply to state-sponsored attacks.

sections.name: Supply Chain, Chips and Hardware
sections.blurb: Cover on the physical inputs. Cargo and transit on high value GPU shipments, foundry concentration risk in Taiwan, thermal shock damage during cooling failure, transformer and switchgear lead times running to four years, secondary market accelerator warranties, delay in startup on fibre trenching, rare earth export bottlenecks, custom silicon logic flaws, pump failures, and cleanroom contamination at packaging plants.

sections.name: Actuarial Science and Underwriting
sections.blurb: How a premium gets calculated for a risk with no claims history. Automated underwriting using vision models and sensor analytics, telemetry-linked dynamic premiums, mandatory red teaming as a condition of cover, parametric payouts triggered by temperature or power thresholds, correlated accumulation modelling when one foundational model serves millions of businesses, governance maturity scoring for discounts, synthetic loss scenarios, third party safety rating agencies, and usage-based policy limits.

sections.name: Regulation, Compliance and D&O
sections.blurb: Where governance failure becomes a claim against a named individual. EU AI Act conformity assessment cover, director and officer liability for failing to oversee AI risk, state-level compliance exposure, greenwashing claims over data centre carbon and power usage effectiveness disclosures, antitrust defence over compute allocation, export control penalties, mandatory liability insurance proposals, workforce displacement suits, data sovereignty fines, and FDA medical software non-compliance.

sections.name: Frontier and Emerging Technology
sections.blurb: Risks being modelled before they are priced. Reinsurance modelling for systemic disruption from unaligned frontier systems, post-quantum migration gaps, autonomous drone fleet liability shifting to cloud infrastructure, brain computer interface software liability, decentralised compute network risk, neuromorphic and optical hardware, AI-assisted synthetic biology and terrorism exclusions, digital twin synchronisation drift, synthetic media stock manipulation, and errors in AI-designed compounds and materials.

sections.name: Insurtech, Captives and Capital Markets
sections.blurb: What happens when traditional carriers decline the risk. Hyperscaler single parent captives self-insuring what nobody will write, parametric micro-insurance on API and GPU availability, startup mutual risk pools, migration of complex AI liability into surplus lines and Lloyds, automated claims processing, catastrophe bonds hedging multi-day cloud outages, insured performance guarantees on model output, generative AI exclusion endorsements, reinsurance capacity caps, and certification-linked discounts.

sections.name: Data Centre Siting, Power and Local Regulation
sections.blurb: Every other framework in this section governs what an AI system may do. This one governs where it may physically exist and what it may draw from the grid, and almost none of it mentions artificial intelligence. Five regimes decide it: state power siting boards, which in many states take exclusive jurisdiction above a megawatt threshold and leave a city able to ask but not require; municipal zoning, which can permit a campus of six million square feet and then prohibit any more, as Fayetteville, Georgia did in March 2026; public utility commissions, which rule on interconnection and on whether data centre load may be recovered from residential customers, as Georgia did when it froze base rates through 2028; environmental permitting, where an air permit may set no carbon limit at all because other pollutants fall below federal thresholds; and infrastructure thresholds, below which no approval is required, which is why an eight-inch gas pipeline serving one customer needs none. The page sets out each regime with the records behind it, the tax abatement terms three municipalities have published, and the four different power figures that siting documents use and directories routinely confuse.

sections.name: Agency Enforcement Actions
sections.blurb: What federal agencies are actually bringing cases over, under powers they already have. An enforcement action is not a law: it is a regulator showing where an existing statute reaches AI today. The DOJ charging algorithmic price coordination under the Sherman Act, the FTC opening a personalised pricing docket, the SEC charging an AI founder with securities fraud. Each one is dated, linked to the agency's own announcement, and tracked as an event rather than a rule.

sections.name: EU, US and China Compared

sections.name: AI Assurance Standards
sections.blurb: Which kind of assurance proves what. A management system certificate under ISO/IEC 42001, audited by bodies under ISO/IEC 17021-1 and 42006, attests to how an organisation governs AI. A model capability test is separate evidence about one system. An impact assessment under ISO/IEC 42005 examines effects on people. Testing laboratories fall under ISO/IEC 17025. This section explains each standard and what its output does and does not show.

sections.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
sections.blurb: The older decisions AI defendants are actually relying on. Every current AI copyright, scraping and defamation case is argued out of a small set of precedents decided long before generative models existed: Sony on substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books on transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ on scraping, Zeran on Section 230. Each profile states what the case held, why AI defendants cite it, and where the analogy is weakest, with a link to the opinion itself.
